strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: making autoregressive models practical for 3D molecule generation with continuous coordinates rather than discretized coordinate tokens.

The proposed system is conceptually coherent: canonical inertial-frame tokenization, RDKit-style canonical atom ordering, geometric attention through RoPE-3D plus a Nyström distance feature, and a hierarchical type-then-coordinate autoregressive objective.

The experimental results are promising on common chemical validity/stability metrics, especially molecule stability on QM9 and B3LYP and the functional-group hit rates in class-conditional generation.
The paper includes useful ablation-motivated design discussion around why RoPE-3D alone may be insufficient and why explicit pairwise distance information is added.
weaknesses: The central invariance/tokenization claim is not fully sound. Inertial-frame canonicalization is ambiguous for molecules with degenerate or near-degenerate inertia eigenvalues, which the paper acknowledges but does not solve rigorously. These cases are chemically common in symmetric molecules, and small perturbations can cause discontinuous canonical frames.

The theorem and proof for resolving axis signs using a fourth point are confusing and appear internally inconsistent: the main text requires a fourth point not on the yz or xz plane, while the appendix states coplanar/non-coplanar conditions inconsistently. It is also unclear how the selected anchor behaves under symmetric ties or numerical noise.

The method depends on RDKit canonical atom ordering from molecular graphs/bonds, but the generation problem is framed as direct 3D atom generation. The paper does not clearly explain how graph/bond information is obtained or avoided during training tokenization, evaluation, and generation, nor whether this leaks information unavailable at generation time.

The evaluation is too narrow to fully support the broad claims. Most results focus on validity, atom stability, molecule stability, and uniqueness; there is little assessment of distributional fidelity, novelty, property distributions, conformer realism, energy/geometry quality, or scaffold/chemical diversity.

The B3LYP comparison is under-supported. Only two baselines are used due to cost, implementation details are missing, and the very poor baseline molecule stability makes it hard to judge whether the comparison reflects model quality, scaling choices, or evaluation/retraining issues.

The controllable generation setup is only lightly validated. The class labels are derived from rule-based functional-group patterns and only the five most frequent classes are evaluated; it is unclear whether the baselines were fairly tuned with the same conditioning mechanism and guidance protocol.

Reproducibility is weak. The manuscript lacks essential details such as architecture sizes, number of layers/heads, anchor selection for Nyström features, diffusion sampler and steps, noise schedule, training schedule, compute budget, hyperparameters, random seeds, and code/data release plan.

Presentation is generally readable but contains repeated preliminary material, equation/notation inconsistencies, and several imprecise claims, such as saying the tokenization is SE(3)-equivariant when the intended property is closer to invariance/canonicalization.

The paper does not include a meaningful limitations or ethics discussion, despite clear practical limitations around chemically valid evaluation, generated molecule misuse, dataset bias, and failure modes for symmetric or chiral molecules.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: bringing autoregressive sequence modeling to 3D molecule generation without discretizing coordinates. The high-level decomposition into atom-type prediction plus continuous coordinate generation is sensible and could be useful if specified and validated more rigorously.

The proposed combination of inertial-frame canonicalization, atom-level tokens, geometry-aware attention, and diffusion loss is a coherent conceptual direction. In particular, using a continuous-coordinate diffusion head avoids the obvious loss of geometric precision caused by coordinate binning.

The manuscript evaluates on several datasets and includes both unconditional and class-conditional generation. The reported numbers, if reproducible, suggest that the approach may improve atom/molecule stability and conditional hit rate over selected baselines.
weaknesses: The central invariance/canonicalization claims are not adequately supported. Inertial-frame alignment is not unique under degenerate or near-degenerate inertia spectra, and the paper largely dismisses symmetric cases as physically equivalent even though an autoregressive model sees different coordinate/token sequences. The fourth-node sign-fixing argument is confusing and inconsistent across the main text and appendix, and it does not convincingly handle linear, planar, symmetric, or nearly symmetric molecules where the chosen anchor may be undefined or numerically unstable.

The atom ordering procedure is underspecified and relies on RDKit canonicalization, but the generated object is a 3D point cloud without known bonds until post hoc bond inference. It is unclear how molecule length, stop tokens, hydrogens, bond perception, and canonical ordering interact during training and sampling. This leaves a major gap in the claimed permutation invariance and in the generative procedure itself.

GeoRoPE/Nystrom is not sufficiently specified to reproduce or verify. The choice and number of anchor points, kernel bandwidth, whether anchors are global or molecule-specific, and how these encodings behave during autoregressive sampling are not described. Some equations are also sloppy or internally inconsistent, such as Eq. 15 repeating the left-hand term, and the derivation of attention scores assumes identity/block structure that is not clearly reconciled with a standard Transformer implementation.

The empirical evidence is too thin for the strength of the claims. There are no ablations isolating inertial canonicalization, canonical atom ordering, RoPE-3D, Nystrom distance encoding, or diffusion loss. Without these, it is impossible to know which component matters or whether the gains come from evaluation details, data preprocessing, or model capacity.

The evaluation is narrow for 3D molecular generation. The paper reports validity, uniqueness, atom stability, and molecule stability, but omits important distributional and chemical-quality metrics such as novelty, property distributions, bond/angle/torsion statistics, energy plausibility, conformer quality, and coverage. Strong claims about chemically plausible 3D generation are therefore not well supported.

Baseline comparison is not fully convincing. On B3LYP, only EDM and Geo2Seq are compared because of computational cost, while the proposed method is trained on a 1M subset; details needed to assess fairness are missing. For conditional generation, only two baselines and five frequent classes are used, which is insufficient to establish state of the art.

Reproducibility is poor. The manuscript lacks essential implementation details: model size, layer counts, optimizer, learning rates, batch sizes, training epochs, sampling steps for the diffusion coordinate head, CFG scales, hardware budget, sample counts, random seeds, variance/error bars, and preprocessing specifics. No code or clear reproducibility package is described.

Presentation quality is uneven. Several sections repeat background material at length while omitting crucial experimental and algorithmic details. The appendix contains broad tutorial material on positional encodings and quaternions, but this does not compensate for missing specifications of the actual method. There are also typographical and mathematical errors that reduce confidence in the technical care.

The limitations and ethics discussion is essentially absent. For a molecule generation paper, the authors should discuss failure modes, instability of canonicalization, invalid or unsafe molecules, potential misuse in chemical design, and limits of functional-group conditioning. The paper instead ends with broad claims about scientific discovery without a balanced limitations treatment.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: making autoregressive modeling viable for 3D molecule generation without discretizing coordinates. The atom-level hybrid token formulation is natural and potentially useful for scalable molecular generation.

The proposed combination of inertial-frame canonicalization, canonical atom ordering, GeoRoPE, Nyström distance features, and diffusion loss for continuous coordinate prediction is coherent and addresses real obstacles in applying Transformers to 3D molecular structures.

Empirical results are strong across several standard metrics. InertialAR improves molecule stability on QM9, atom stability on GEOM-Drugs, and substantially outperforms EDM and Geo2Seq on the reported B3LYP-1M benchmark, especially in molecule stability.

The class-conditional generation experiment is a useful extension beyond unconditional generation. The functional-group class construction and hit-rate evaluation give evidence that the model can support targeted chemical generation rather than only sample plausible molecules.
The presentation is generally clear, with helpful figures and appendices explaining the geometry, Nyström approximation, and diffusion-loss background.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is a major weakness. The manuscript does not provide sufficient implementation detail: model size, number of layers/heads, diffusion sampling steps, optimizer, learning rates, training compute, batch sizes, anchor-point choices for Nyström, number of generated samples, seeds, or variance/error bars are largely absent. This makes the reported gains hard to verify.

The canonicalization argument is not fully convincing. Inertial frames are ambiguous for degenerate or near-degenerate eigenvalues, which are common in symmetric molecules, and the paper mostly dismisses these as physically equivalent. However, autoregressive likelihood and generated coordinate sequences depend on a unique canonical pose. The fourth-node sign-fixing procedure also has unclear behavior for planar, linear, highly symmetric, or numerically unstable cases.

The theorem/proof around frame direction determination is confusing and contains inconsistencies: the main text says the fourth point should not lie on the yz or xz plane, while the appendix theorem refers to a point being coplanar/non-coplanar in contradictory ways. This weakens confidence in the claimed guarantee of unique canonical tokenization.

The experimental evaluation lacks ablations. It is unclear how much of the gain comes from inertial canonicalization, RDKit canonical ordering, RoPE-3D, Nyström features, diffusion loss, model size, or training budget. Since the method is a combination of several components, this is a significant evidential gap.

The comparisons may not be fully fair or complete. B3LYP uses only two baselines due to computational cost, and the exact subset construction is unspecified. Conditional baselines are compared only for selected frequent classes, and it is unclear whether EDM and Geo2Seq were adapted and tuned with comparable care for classifier-free guidance and the reconstructed labels.

The paper does not discuss limitations or ethics in a substantive way. For molecule generation, dual-use risks, validity beyond RDKit heuristics, synthetic accessibility, and downstream experimental validation are relevant. The absence of a limitations discussion is notable, especially given the strong claims about scientific discovery.

Some claims are overstated relative to the evidence. For example, the conclusion gestures toward foundation-model potential and protein/material extension, but the experiments remain limited to relatively standard molecular validity metrics and do not evaluate property optimization, novelty against training data in depth, synthesis feasibility, or quantum-chemical accuracy of generated conformers.

strengths: The paper tackles a meaningful gap: making autoregressive models practical for 3D molecule generation without discretizing coordinates. The atom-level tokenization plus hierarchical type/coordinate prediction is a coherent framing of the problem.

The method is conceptually simple and potentially useful. Inertial-frame canonicalization, RDKit-based atom ordering, geometry-aware attention, and diffusion loss for continuous coordinates fit together naturally and are well motivated.

The reported empirical results are strong on standard validity/stability metrics. InertialAR improves several QM9, GEOM-Drugs, and B3LYP metrics, and the conditional generation results show large gains in functional-group hit rate over EDM and Geo2Seq.

The paper includes some relevant ablations and robustness checks: diffusion loss versus L2 regression, canonical atom indexing, perturbation sensitivity, and principal-moment degeneracy frequency. These help support the design choices.
The manuscript is generally readable, with clear high-level figures and a useful related-work discussion positioning canonicalization relative to equivariant and invariant approaches.
The impact statement appropriately notes possible misuse in hazardous compound generation and calls for safety screening and regulatory safeguards.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is a major weakness. The abstract says code is available but gives no URL, and the manuscript lacks essential details such as architecture sizes, optimizer settings, training schedules, sampling steps for the coordinate diffusion head, guidance scales, number of generated samples, random seeds, and compute budget.

Several central claims are stronger than the evidence supports. The paper claims efficiency and flexibility advantages over diffusion models, but gives no runtime, sampling-cost, memory, or scaling comparison. Because coordinates are still generated through iterative denoising at each autoregressive step, the efficiency claim is especially important to quantify.

The evaluation is too narrow for 3D molecule generation. Validity, uniqueness, atom stability, and molecule stability are useful but insufficient; the paper does not report novelty, diversity beyond uniqueness, distributional similarity, property distributions, energy/geometry quality, conformer realism, or failure cases. High valency-based validity alone does not establish chemically useful generation.

Baseline comparisons are incomplete or insufficiently controlled. On B3LYP the paper compares only EDM and Geo2Seq despite making broad SOTA claims, and it does not specify whether baselines were retrained with comparable capacity, tuned fairly, or evaluated under identical sample budgets. Conditional generation compares only two baselines and uses a newly constructed labeling task whose details are under-specified.

The canonicalization method is useful but not as cleanly “unique” as claimed. Inertial frames have degeneracies and discontinuities; the paper acknowledges rare dataset degeneracy but handles it by excluding molecules, which weakens the claim of a general invariant tokenization. The farthest-anchor sign rule also depends on tie-breaking and nonzero projected coordinates, and its behavior for generated or highly symmetric molecules is not fully analyzed.

The RDKit canonical ordering step relies on molecular connectivity/canonical SMILES, but the paper does not clearly explain how this interacts with datasets, hydrogens, stereochemistry, tied ranks, or generated coordinate-only outputs. This is central to the permutation-invariance claim and needs a more precise algorithmic specification.

The conditional generation setup is not sufficiently documented. The predefined SMARTS functional group library, pattern-to-ID mapping, class frequencies, train/test leakage considerations, and target selection rationale are not provided, making the large hit-rate improvements difficult to independently assess.

Ablations are limited. The paper does not isolate ManhattanPE versus EuclideanPE, Nyström anchor count and bandwidth choices, block-diagonal projection design, atom-ordering alternatives, inertial frame versus other canonical frames, or the hierarchical factorization itself.

The B3LYP results show very low molecule stability even for InertialAR (24.7%), despite being presented as a strong success. This suggests the model still struggles substantially at scale, and the discussion does not adequately contextualize that limitation.

Presentation has some overclaiming and missing polish: the code link is blank, some equations and terminology are imprecise, and the paper repeatedly states state-of-the-art performance while some metrics are not best and some comparisons are limited.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: adapting autoregressive sequence models to 3D molecule generation while respecting SE(3) and atom-index symmetries.

The combination of inertial-frame canonicalization, deterministic atom ordering, geometry-aware attention, and diffusion loss for continuous coordinates is coherent at a high level and targets real obstacles in AR molecular generation.
The manuscript includes comparisons on QM9, GEOM-Drugs, and a larger B3LYP subset, plus some ablations for diffusion loss, canonical atom indexing, and inertial-frame stability.
weaknesses: The empirical evidence is not strong enough to support the broad claims. The evaluation mostly reports validity, uniqueness, atom stability, and molecule stability, but does not adequately measure distributional fidelity, novelty versus memorization, property distributions, conformer quality/energy, diversity beyond uniqueness, or realistic downstream usefulness. This is especially concerning for an autoregressive model trained on canonical sequences, where memorization and ordering effects should be carefully ruled out.

Reproducibility is weak. The manuscript says code is available but the link is blank, and key implementation details are missing or underspecified, including Transformer size, training budget, sampling settings, number of generated molecules, diffusion sampling steps per atom, Nystrom anchor selection, RBF bandwidth, CFG/dropout settings, and exact B3LYP subset construction.

The claimed efficiency advantage over diffusion models is not demonstrated. The coordinate decoder itself uses iterative diffusion sampling for every atom, yet the paper does not report sampling speed, number of denoising steps, memory, or latency. This undermines one of the main motivations for using an autoregressive formulation.

The novelty is limited and somewhat overstated. Inertial/PCA frames, canonical molecular ordering, RoPE-like relative encodings, Nystrom kernel features, classifier-free guidance, and diffusion loss for continuous AR tokens are all existing ideas. The paper presents a useful combination, but it does not clearly isolate a new technical contribution or provide deep analysis showing why this composition works beyond the ablations.

The B3LYP results are not convincing as evidence of scalability or state of the art. Only EDM and Geo2Seq are compared, the selected 1M subset is insufficiently specified, and the molecule stability remains very low at 24.7%, despite being described as a dramatic success.

The class-conditional generation setup is not well justified. The authors create functional-group class IDs via rule-based SMARTS matching and evaluate only the five most frequent classes on QM9. This may be a narrow and favorable benchmark, and the paper does not provide enough detail about class balance, train/test splits by class, leakage risks, or whether generated structures are novel rather than close variants of training molecules.

Some central technical claims are stronger than the method warrants. The tokenization is described as producing a unique SE(3)- and permutation-invariant sequence, but inertial-frame degeneracies, sign discontinuities, symmetric molecules, and RDKit canonicalization ties are only partially handled. Excluding degenerate molecules is a pragmatic workaround, not a complete solution.

The ablation study is too thin. It tests diffusion loss and atom ordering, but does not isolate GeoPE components, inertial-frame canonicalization versus alternatives, anchor choices for EuclideanPE, model scale, sampling steps, or whether gains come from the coordinate diffusion decoder rather than the proposed tokenization/attention design.

Presentation is generally readable, but several claims are inflated relative to the evidence, such as suggesting foundation-model potential or broad robustness from limited benchmark results. The paper would benefit from a more cautious framing and more complete experimental reporting.

The ethics/limitations discussion is minimal. The paper briefly mentions hazardous compound generation, but does not seriously discuss false validity signals, misuse through generated toxic molecules, dataset bias, memorization of known compounds, or the safety implications of controllable functional-group generation.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important problem: making autoregressive models viable for 3D molecule generation, where SE(3) symmetry, atom-order ambiguity, and continuous coordinate prediction are genuine obstacles.

The proposed system is technically coherent. Inertial-frame canonicalization gives a simple generation-oriented tokenization, GeoPE injects both axis-wise relative geometry and approximate Euclidean distance information into attention, and the hierarchical atom-type-then-coordinate decoder is a natural fit for hybrid discrete/continuous molecular tokens.

The empirical results are strong overall. InertialAR is competitive or best on most QM9 and GEOM-Drugs metrics, and the B3LYP-1M results show a large advantage over EDM and Geo2Seq, especially in validity and molecule stability.

The controllable generation experiments are a meaningful addition. The functional-group conditioning setup and hit-rate metric demonstrate that the approach is not only producing valid molecules but can also steer generation toward target chemical functionality.

The paper includes useful robustness and ablation evidence: inertial-frame degeneracy appears rare in QM9/Drugs, perturbation-induced anchor changes are uncommon at realistic noise scales, diffusion loss is clearly superior to direct L2 coordinate regression, and canonical atom indexing modestly improves generation quality.

Presentation is generally clear. The main method is easy to follow, the appendix gives helpful derivations for Nyström EuclideanPE and sign disambiguation, and the impact statement acknowledges dual-use risks in molecule generation.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is not yet fully satisfactory. The manuscript lacks many implementation details needed to independently reproduce the results, including model size, optimizer settings, training compute, sampling procedure, diffusion denoising steps, anchor selection details for EuclideanPE, exact B3LYP subset construction, and code/data release information; the abstract says code is available but the link appears blank.

The ablation coverage is incomplete relative to the claimed contributions. There is no clear component-wise ablation of ManhattanPE vs EuclideanPE, inertial-frame canonicalization vs alternative canonicalization or augmentation, hierarchical decoding vs a less structured decoder, or CFG design choices in conditional generation.

Some comparisons are only partially controlled. On B3LYP, the paper compares only against EDM and Geo2Seq because of cost, which is understandable but weakens the breadth of the SOTA claim. Across QM9/GEOM-Drugs, the baselines differ substantially in architecture, training setup, and possibly implementation protocol.

The central canonicalization idea is useful but not entirely original: inertial/PCA frames and canonicalization are well established in molecular and geometric learning. The novelty is mainly the integration into an autoregressive 3D molecule generator, plus the GeoPE/decoder design, rather than a fundamentally new symmetry-handling principle.

The evaluation emphasizes standard validity, uniqueness, and stability metrics, but provides limited deeper chemical assessment. There is little analysis of diversity beyond uniqueness, distributional matching, novelty against training molecules, property distributions, energy plausibility, synthesizability, or failure cases.

The robustness analysis is helpful but narrow. Measuring farthest-atom identity changes and exact principal-moment degeneracy does not fully address discontinuities in canonical frames, near-symmetric molecules, sensitivity during generation, or how excluded degenerate molecules affect broader deployment.

The ethics discussion correctly flags hazardous compound generation but remains high-level. A stronger paper would include more concrete safety evaluation or filtering discussion, especially since controllable functional-group generation could increase dual-use concerns.
